implementation_notes: The .NET framework ships System.Transactions, and it is worth naming the trap explicitly: TransactionScope is a *distributed resource* coordinator with an ambient transaction, enlistment, two-phase commit and a transaction manager - it is the Unit of Work pattern over resources, not in-memory transactional memory. Using it to protect a shared `List<T>` or a dictionary is a category error and costs far more than the operation. The honest realisation is the hand-written validate-then-act loop over `Interlocked.CompareExchange`, wrapped once in a small `Txn` helper so the discipline lives in one place: read into locals, compute, attempt the CAS, and on failure re-read every location the block depends on and start over. Because C# gives you immutable records and reference-typed handles, a slightly better shape is available than in C - keep the transactional state in an immutable record and swap the whole reference with `Interlocked.Exchange`, which makes rollback trivial (keep the old reference) and makes 'changed' a reference comparison.
pitfalls: Reaching for TransactionScope to guard in-memory collections: it enlists resources, may promote to a distributed transaction, and is vastly more expensive than the CAS loop it replaces.
Interlocked operations on fields of a mutable object are not atomic with respect to each other - two CAS calls on one object can interleave, which is exactly the compensation problem STM removes.
Volatile.Read for a reference field gives you a consistent reference but not the consistency of the object's fields; snapshot the whole immutable object or lock.
async/await inside the retry loop makes each attempt suspend, widening the conflict window; keep the loop synchronous and non-blocking.
Swallowing the failed CAS and returning as if it succeeded, which silently loses the update.
